source.title: Monitoring Fatigue Status in Elite Team-Sport Athletes: Implications for Practice

paper.citation: Thorpe, R. T., Atkinson, G., Drust, B., & Gregson, W. (2017). Monitoring fatigue status in elite team-sport athletes: Implications for practice. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance, 12(Suppl 2), S2-27–S2-34. https://doi.org/10.1123/ijspp.2016-0434
paper.abstract: Which practical measures may help monitor fatigue in elite team-sport athletes, and how should practitioners distinguish detectable change from meaningful change? This is a narrative brief review of team-sport fatigue monitoring, supplemented with evidence from other sports where team-sport evidence was unavailable. Much of the applied evidence discussed comes from elite association football, Australian football, rugby, and endurance sport; it is not specific to collegiate American football. The authors narratively review athlete self-report, heart-rate-derived, physical-performance, range-of-motion, and biochemical measures and discuss reliability, validity, and minimal clinically important difference (MCID). No systematic-search strategy, eligibility criteria, risk-of-bias assessment, or quantitative synthesis is reported, so conclusions reflect a selective review rather than a systematic estimate.
paper.tldr: This brief review provides a measurement-focused framework for selecting fatigue-monitoring tools and deciding whether an observed change is both larger than measurement noise and practically meaningful. Athlete self-report measures appeared responsive to acute and chronic load in several team-sport studies, but the authors state that further work is needed to establish relationships with injury and illness. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: The authors narratively review athlete self-report, heart-rate-derived, physical-performance, range-of-motion, and biochemical measures and discuss reliability, validity, and minimal clinically important difference (MCID). No systematic-search strategy, eligibility criteria, risk-of-bias assessment, or quantitative synthesis is reported, so conclusions reflect a selective review rather than a systematic estimate.
paper.findings: Athlete self-report measures appeared responsive to acute and chronic load in several team-sport studies, but the authors state that further work is needed to establish relationships with injury and illness. Submaximal exercise heart rate, HRV, and heart-rate recovery showed inconsistent or context-dependent responses; the direction of heart-rate changes should not be interpreted as fatigue in isolation. Countermovement-jump height alone may be insensitive to training-load changes, while alternative force–time variables may capture neuromuscular changes; prospective team-sport validation remained limited. A minimal detectable change is not the same as an MCID: observed change should be considered against within-athlete measurement error and an externally justified practical anchor. The authors recommend noninvasive, time-efficient tools and a combination of subjective and objective measures because fatigue is multifactorial and no single measure adequately explains athlete status.
paper.limitations: This is a 2017 narrative review; evidence selection is not reproducible and newer measurement, wearable, and modeling research may change the balance of evidence. Sensitivity to prior training load does not establish that a measure predicts subsequent performance, injury, illness, or availability. Many cited findings are correlational, sport-specific, and based on small applied samples; physiological markers can shift for reasons other than fatigue, including fitness, heat, plasma-volume changes, and measurement timing. MCID selection in team sport is difficult because performance is multicomponent and variable, and athlete, coach, and organization may value different anchors. The review does not validate universal thresholds or justify making high-stakes participation decisions from a single metric.
paper.practicalImplications: Build a fatigue-monitoring system around a defined decision, standardized measurement process, within-athlete reliability, and a meaningful external anchor. Use trends and converging subjective and objective information, then investigate context before changing training. For collegiate American football, calibrate measures within position, season phase, and testing conditions; do not import soccer-derived thresholds or treat a statistically unusual value as injury prediction.
